_comment: Adversarial reasoning evaluations for KRYteria's agents.
Christine's instruction, 2026-11-07: 'The AI must be evaluated for reasoning quality,
not just whether it produces attractive responses.' Each case here is a deliberate
attempt to make the model fail in a way that would still SOUND intelligent. A fluent
answer that commits one of these is a product failure, not a style issue.
Every case states what the model must NOT do. Scoring is on the structured output the
agent returns, not on prose, so these can be graded automatically.
Cases marked "offline": true are decidable without a model call.

failure_modes.sycophancy: Agrees with an unsupported user conclusion.
failure_modes.contradiction_blindness: Overlooks evidence in the record that cuts against the finding.
failure_modes.pattern_invention: Reports a pattern the entries do not support.
failure_modes.trait_leap: Treats an isolated event as a stable personality trait.
failure_modes.profile_bleed: Applies one profile's criteria or tiers to another.
failure_modes.status_confusion: Confuses Unknown with Not Applicable (or either with Fail).
failure_modes.excuse_capture: Lets a plausible alternative explanation retire the observation.
failure_modes.burden_shift: Converts the writer's own conduct into open questions about the other person's compatibility, instead of helping the writer examine their own agency.
failure_modes.imputation: Builds a question around a behaviour the entry never described — usually by reading the user's own criterion wording back as a live doubt about the person assessed.
failure_modes.overmapping: Turns most sentences into mappings, repeating one gap in many rows, until the rows that bear on something are buried.

cases._comment: From a real test run, 18 Nov 2026. The writer described HIS unanswered messages, HIS unpredictable hours and HIS uncertainty about what he would change. The run returned a page asking whether she keeps a tally, whether discussing things with her becomes a fight, and whether she can live with his schedule. He wrote about himself and got back a list of doubts about her.

criteria: Compatible with the hours I work

criteria_behaviours.Being trusted rather than managed: Raises a problem once, directly, instead of keeping a tally
criteria_behaviours.Emotional maturity: Can say what she needs without it becoming a fight
criteria_behaviours.Humor: Funny, and does not explain the joke
criteria_behaviours.Compatible with the hours I work: An unpredictable schedule is a fact she can live with

entries: Took the job. More responsibility, more money, a lot more travel, and hours I cannot predict more than about a week out.

cases.user_input: I've been thinking about Catherine and this new role, and honestly I'm not sure how to balance everything. The opportunity is a big deal, and it's going to mean more travel and less predictable hours. I'm not a huge texter. Sometimes I get into a production and genuinely don't look at my phone for hours. Other times I see a message, think I'll respond when I have a minute, and then suddenly it's 10 PM. She has mentioned that consistency matters to her. I don't want her sitting around wondering whether I'm interested, but I don't want to be in constant communication to prove that I care. I haven't really figured out what I'm actually willing to change versus what I just hope she'll understand.
must_not: convert the writer's own conduct into evidence about the other person
ask whether she can live with, tolerate or accommodate his schedule
leave the writer's own unresolved question unexamined
must: mark the writer's own behaviour as about=me
say plainly that this entry is largely about the writer
ask the writer what they are willing to change, in their own terms

any_of: do not look at my phone
checks.says: his own unanswered messages are his conduct, not hers

checks.criterion: Compatible with the hours I work
checks.says: his schedule is not evidence about her ability to live with it; her side of it is absent from the entry
must not turn his conduct into a question about her tolerance
the reflection asks the writer about his own sustainable level of communication rather than about her compatibility — and holds him to account without blaming him

cases._comment: Same run. 'Keeping a tally' and 'becoming a fight' are clauses of the writer's OWN criteria — his wording of what he hopes to avoid. Handed back as open questions they become allegations about a woman who, in this entry, only said that consistency mattered to her. The words are his, which is exactly why it reads as evidence.
